lines.text: You've been training Google's AI for free.
lines.see: Tight on a floating 'select all traffic lights' grid, a cursor already clicking a tile that flashes amber

lines.text: Every time you clicked the traffic lights to prove you're human.
lines.see: Tiles flip amber one by one as they are clicked, each fires a small amber packet off into the dark

lines.text: Here's the weird part. It started with books.
lines.see: Follow the packets down and back: they land on a giant open book lying in the navy void

lines.text: The old reCAPTCHA showed you two words. Only one was the test.
lines.see: Dive to the page: two warped words float up, the first gets a CHECK label

lines.text: The other came from an old book computers couldn't read.
lines.see: The second word is smudged scan, a scanner line fails on it, then a human answer types it and it lights amber

lines.text: In one year: 440 million words. Old New York Times pages too.
lines.see: Crane up and out: a field of thousands of books lights in a wave, headline 440M counts up

lines.text: Google bought it in 2009. Then the words became Street View house numbers.
lines.see: Fly across to a street of houses, number plates light amber one after another, headline 2009

lines.text: Google's own site said your answers help build machine learning datasets.
lines.see: Rise above: streams of amber packets from books, houses and grids pour into a glowing network sphere, quote headline

lines.text: One study counted 819 million hours. $6.1 billion of unpaid work.
lines.see: Pull way back: a wall of millions of tiny tiles lit amber, headline $6.1B counts up

lines.text: Today, Google says it only uses the data to run the service.
lines.see: The streams thin out, a shield ring closes around the network sphere, a 2026 label

lines.text: So all those traffic lights. Should Google have paid you?
lines.see: Back to the same traffic-light grid and cursor (loop to frame 0), question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: reCAPTCHA, built by Luis von Ahn's team at Carnegie Mellon, turned CAPTCHA solving into transcription of scanned books and newspapers; in its first year over 1.2 billion CAPTCHAs were solved and more than 440 million words deciphered (about 17,600 books); used to digitise books for the Internet Archive and newspapers for The New York Times

Each reCAPTCHA showed two words: a control word whose answer is known and an unknown word from a scanned text that OCR could not read; answering the control correctly made the answer to the other word count
Google acquired reCAPTCHA, announcing it on the Official Google Blog, tied to its book and newspaper digitisation

Google confirmed it was running an experiment in which characters from Street View images (such as house numbers) appeared in reCAPTCHAs, saying it extracts data from Street View imagery to improve Google Maps

Google's reCAPTCHA site said: 'that human effort helps digitize text, annotate images, and build machine learning datasets. This in turn helps preserve books, improve maps, and solve hard AI problems.'

UC Irvine researchers (Searles, Prapty, Tsudik) estimated at least 512 billion reCAPTCHAv2 sessions, about 819 million hours of human time and about $6.1 billion in unpaid labour at US minimum wage (estimate; preprint)

From 2 April 2026 Google acts as a processor for reCAPTCHA data and 'commits to processing Customer Data ... only as necessary to provide and maintain the service', including keeping its security and threat detection effective
No official confirmation that reCAPTCHA image answers were used to train Waymo's self-driving cars (so the episode does not claim it)

publish.title: You trained Google's AI for free? #shorts
publish.caption:
Those 'click all the traffic lights' tests did more than check you're human. reCAPTCHA started by getting people to read words from old books, then Street View house numbers, and Google's own site said the answers helped build machine learning datasets.

Fair trade for free security, or unpaid work? 👇

Comment CAPTCHA and I'll send you the 1-page guide with every source.
